claim: Drosophila melanogaster contains sweet- and bitter-sensing cells in multiple organs, including external organs such as the legs and labellum and internal organs such as the pharynx.
source: Flies contain sweet- and bitter-sensing cells in multiple organs, including external organs such as the legs and labellum (the distal segment of the proboscis, the fly's feeding organ) and internal organs such as the pharynx (Scott, 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scott, 2018 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Sweet- and bitter-sensing neurons within a single organ exhibit functional diversity.
source: Sweet- and bitter-sensing neurons within a single organ also exhibit functional diversity (Scott, 2018; Weiss et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2014; Fujii et al., 2015; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The labellum contains four classes of bitter-sensing neurons (S-a, S-b, I-a, and I-b), defined by the gustatory receptors (Grs) that they express.
source: For example, the labellum contains four classes of bitter-sensing neurons (S-a, S-b, I-a, and I-b), defined by the gustatory receptors(Grs) that they express, and these classes show different response profiles to bitter tastants (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: The four classes of bitter-sensing neurons in the labellum show different response profiles to bitter tastants.
source: For example, the labellum contains four classes of bitter-sensing neurons (S-a, S-b, I-a, and I-b), defined by the gustatory receptors(Grs) that they express, and these classes show different response profiles to bitter tastants (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: Taste neurons in different organs have different behavioral roles for appetitive tastes.
source: Previous work, focusing mainly on appetitive tastes, suggests that taste neurons in different organs have different behavioral roles (Thoma et al., 2016; Murata et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Appetitive tastes such as sugar elicit a sequence of behaviors, with specific organs regulating each step.
source: Appetitive tastes such as sugar elicit a sequence of behaviors, with specific organs regulating each step (Dethier, 1976; Scott, 2018; Mahishi and Huetteroth, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Flies first detect the presence of sugar with their legs.
source: Flies first detect the presence of sugar with their legs.
evidence: The claim is stated as part of a description of the sequence of sugar-elicited behaviors.

claim: Taste detection by the leg may cause the fly to stop walking and extend its proboscis to contact the food, depending on the sugar concentration and the fly's hunger state.
source: Depending on the sugar concentration and the fly's hunger state, taste detection by the leg may cause the fly to stop walking and extend its proboscis to contact the food.
evidence: The claim is stated as part of a description of the sequence of sugar-elicited behaviors.

claim: Labellar taste stimulation may trigger the initiation of food consumption.
source: Labellar taste stimulation may then trigger the initiation of food consumption.
evidence: The claim is stated as part of a description of the sequence of sugar-elicited behaviors.

claim: Pharyngeal taste neurons regulate the duration of food ingestion.
source: Food consumption leads to stimulation of pharyngeal taste neurons, which regulate the duration of food ingestion (LeDue et al., 2015; Yapici et al., 2016; Joseph et al., 2017) and elicit local search behavior to find more food (Murata et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Pharyngeal taste neurons elicit local search behavior to find more food.
source: Food consumption leads to stimulation of pharyngeal taste neurons, which regulate the duration of food ingestion (LeDue et al., 2015; Yapici et al., 2016; Joseph et al., 2017) and elicit local search behavior to find more food (Murata et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Murata et al., 2017.

claim: Sugar-sensing inputs from different organs appear to be processed separately to regulate different aspects of behavior.
source: Thus, sugar-sensing inputs from different organs appear to be processed separately to regulate different aspects of behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the preceding description of organ-specific roles in sugar taste processing.

claim: Some studies suggest that different types of bitter neurons have different behavioral roles.
source: However, it is not clear whether the same principle applies to aversive tastes such as bitter. Some studies suggest that different types of bitter neurons have different behavioral roles (Joseph and Heberlein, 2012; Chen et al., 2019), but this has not been widely examined.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Joseph and Heberlein, 2012 and Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Bitter-sensing neurons in different organs project axons to different regions of the subesophageal zone (SEZ).
source: The anatomical organization of sensory projections also suggests the possibility of segregated processing: bitter-sensing neurons in different organs project axons to different regions of the subesophageal zone (SEZ), the primary taste area of the brain, suggesting potential connections to distinct downstream pathways (Wang et al., 2004; Kwon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2004 and Kwon et al., 2014.

claim: Bitter-sensing neurons in different organs show different response dynamics.
source: Finally, the observation that bitter-sensing neurons in different organs show different response dynamics suggests that these neurons may have distinct functional roles (Devineni et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Devineni et al., 2021.

claim: Bitter neuron subsets elicited a broad and highly overlapping set of behaviors, suggesting that these inputs converge onto common downstream pathways.
source: First, we optogenetically activated subsets of bitter neurons within each organ. These subsets elicited broad and highly overlapping behavioral effects, suggesting that they converge onto common downstream pathways, but we also observed behavioral differences that argue for biased convergence.
evidence: The claim is supported by the optogenetic activation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Behavioral differences observed upon activating bitter neuron subsets argue for biased convergence.
source: First, we optogenetically activated subsets of bitter neurons within each organ. These subsets elicited broad and highly overlapping behavioral effects, suggesting that they converge onto common downstream pathways, but we also observed behavioral differences that argue for biased convergence.
evidence: The claim is supported by the optogenetic activation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Bitter neurons in different organs connect to overlapping downstream pathways with biased connectivity.
source: Consistent with these results, transsynaptic tracing revealed that bitter neurons in different organs connect to overlapping downstream pathways with biased connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: mlSEZt neurons integrate input from multiple organs.
source: We investigated taste processing in one type of downstream bitter neuron that projects to the higher brain. These neurons integrate input from multiple organs and regulate specific taste-related behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments characterizing mlSEZt neurons described in the manuscript.

claim: mlSEZt neurons regulate specific taste-related behaviors.
source: We investigated taste processing in one type of downstream bitter neuron that projects to the higher brain. These neurons integrate input from multiple organs and regulate specific taste-related behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral experiments with mlSEZt neurons described in the manuscript.

claim: Different bitter inputs are selectively integrated early in the circuit, enabling the pooling of information.
source: Together, these results reveal that different bitter inputs are selectively integrated early in the circuit, enabling the pooling of information, while the circuit then diverges into multiple pathways that may have different roles.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The bitter taste circuit diverges into multiple pathways that may have different roles.
source: Together, these results reveal that different bitter inputs are selectively integrated early in the circuit, enabling the pooling of information, while the circuit then diverges into multiple pathways that may have different roles.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Different mechanoreceptor neurons detect different types of touch.
source: For instance, different mechanoreceptor neurons detect different types of touch (Abraira and Ginty, 2013) and different types of cones detect distinct wavelengths of light (Rushton, 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abraira and Ginty, 2013.

claim: Different types of cones detect distinct wavelengths of light.
source: For instance, different mechanoreceptor neurons detect different types of touch (Abraira and Ginty, 2013) and different types of cones detect distinct wavelengths of light (Rushton, 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rushton, 1972.

claim: Gr33a-Gal4 labels all bitter-sensing neurons across the body.
source: We used previously characterized Gal4 lines (Weiss et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2014; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017) to target all bitter-sensing neurons across the body (Gr33a-Gal4) as well as four subsets of bitter neurons within specific organs (Figure 1C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of Gal4 lines used in the study and citations to previous characterizations.

claim: Gr58c-Gal4 labels bitter neurons in the leg.
source: We used previously characterized Gal4 lines (Weiss et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2014; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017) to target all bitter-sensing neurons across the body (Gr33a-Gal4) as well as four subsets of bitter neurons within specific organs (Figure 1C–D): (1) bitter neurons in the leg (Gr58c-Gal4)
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of Gal4 lines used in the study and citations to previous characterizations.

claim: Gr59c-Gal4 labels bitter neurons in the labellum belonging to classes S-a and I-a.
source: We used previously characterized Gal4 lines (Weiss et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2014; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017) to target all bitter-sensing neurons across the body (Gr33a-Gal4) as well as four subsets of bitter neurons within specific organs (Figure 1C–D): (1) bitter neurons in the leg (Gr58c-Gal4); (2) bitter neurons in the labellum belonging to classes S-a and I-a (Gr59c-Gal4)
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of Gal4 lines used in the study and citations to previous characterizations.

claim: Gr22f-Gal4 labels bitter neurons in the labellum belonging to class S-b.
source: We used previously characterized Gal4 lines (Weiss et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2014; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017) to target all bitter-sensing neurons across the body (Gr33a-Gal4) as well as four subsets of bitter neurons within specific organs (Figure 1C–D): (1) bitter neurons in the leg (Gr58c-Gal4); (2) bitter neurons in the labellum belonging to classes S-a and I-a (Gr59c-Gal4); (3) bitter neurons in the labellum belonging to class S-b (Gr22f-Gal4)
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of Gal4 lines used in the study and citations to previous characterizations.

claim: Gr9a-Gal4 labels a pharyngeal bitter neuron termed V6.
source: We used previously characterized Gal4 lines (Weiss et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2014; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017) to target all bitter-sensing neurons across the body (Gr33a-Gal4) as well as four subsets of bitter neurons within specific organs (Figure 1C–D): (1) bitter neurons in the leg (Gr58c-Gal4); (2) bitter neurons in the labellum belonging to classes S-a and I-a (Gr59c-Gal4); (3) bitter neurons in the labellum belonging to class S-b (Gr22f-Gal4); and (4) a pharyngeal bitter neuron termed V6 (Gr9a-Gal4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of Gal4 lines used in the study and citations to previous characterizations.

claim: The expression patterns of the four Gal4 lines have been carefully validated by previous studies, showing that each line is expressed in only one of the three taste organs under study (leg, labellum, or pharynx).
source: The expression patterns of these four Gal4 lines have been carefully validated by previous studies, showing that each line is expressed in only one of the three taste organs under study (leg, labellum, or pharynx) (Weiss et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2014; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies that validated the expression patterns.

claim: Chrimson has been previously used to activate taste sensory neurons.
source: We used the light-activated channel Chrimson to drive neuronal activation (Klapoetke et al., 2014). Chrimson has been previously used to activate taste sensory neurons (Klapoetke et al., 2014; Musso et al., 2019; Moreira et al., 2019), and bitter-sensing neurons expressing Chrimson are effectively activated by red light (Devineni et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Klapoetke et al., 2014, Musso et al., 2019, and Moreira et al., 2019.

claim: Bitter-sensing neurons expressing Chrimson are effectively activated by red light.
source: We used the light-activated channel Chrimson to drive neuronal activation (Klapoetke et al., 2014). Chrimson has been previously used to activate taste sensory neurons (Klapoetke et al., 2014; Musso et al., 2019; Moreira et al., 2019), and bitter-sensing neurons expressing Chrimson are effectively activated by red light (Devineni et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Devineni et al., 2021.

claim: Activating the entire population of bitter-sensing neurons strongly suppressed PER to sugar.
source: As expected, activating the entire population of bitter-sensing neurons strongly suppressed PER to sugar (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Activating any of the four bitter neuron subsets suppressed PER to a similar extent.
source: Interestingly, activating any of the four bitter neuron subsets also suppressed PER to a similar extent (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Subsets of bitter neurons within any of the three organs – the leg, labellum, or pharynx – can suppress the initiation of feeding.
source: Thus, subsets of bitter neurons within any of the three organs – the leg, labellum, or pharynx – can suppress the initiation of feeding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PER suppression results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Activating all bitter-sensing neurons or any of the four subsets caused a near-complete suppression of feeding.
source: Activating all bitter-sensing neurons or any of the four subsets caused a near-complete suppression of feeding (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C–D.

claim: All four bitter neuron subsets suppressed the total feeding duration, number of feeding bouts, sip number, and sip duration.
source: All four bitter neuron subsets suppressed the total feeding duration, number of feeding bouts, sip number, and sip duration (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The number of feeding bursts was suppressed by all subsets except for leg neurons, although they showed the same trend.
source: The number of feeding bursts was suppressed by all subsets except for leg neurons, although they showed the same trend (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The duration of individual feeding bouts was suppressed by only one subset, the pharyngeal neurons, suggesting that this specific parameter may be primarily regulated by the pharynx.
source: The duration of individual feeding bouts was suppressed by only one subset, the pharyngeal neurons, suggesting that this specific parameter may be primarily regulated by the pharynx (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and represents an inference about the role of pharyngeal neurons.

claim: Silencing all bitter neurons across the body strongly increased feeding.
source: As expected, silencing all bitter neurons across the body strongly increased feeding (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F–G.

claim: Silencing two of the four subsets (neurons in the leg and pharynx) increased feeding in experimental flies, with pharyngeal neurons showing a stronger effect.
source: Silencing two of the four subsets (neurons in the leg and pharynx) increased feeding in experimental flies, with pharyngeal neurons showing a stronger effect (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The effects of light stimulation generally did not reach statistical significance when compared with genetic controls for silencing experiments.
source: However, the effects of light stimulation generally did not reach statistical significance when compared with genetic controls (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Activating each bitter neuron subset had strong effects on feeding whereas silencing had weaker or null effects.
source: Thus, activating each bitter neuron subset had strong effects on feeding whereas silencing had weaker or null effects.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the feeding activation and silencing results.

claim: Different bitter neuron subsets act in a parallel and partially redundant manner to regulate feeding.
source: These results suggest that different bitter neuron subsets act in a parallel and partially redundant manner to regulate feeding, implying that these input channels are integrated by downstream feeding circuits.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the feeding activation and silencing results.

claim: Activating the entire population of bitter neurons strongly stimulated locomotion at all light intensities.
source: Activating the entire population of bitter neurons strongly stimulated locomotion at all light intensities. Light onset elicited a transient increase in turning and a more sustained increase in forward velocity and the fraction of flies moving (Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Light onset elicited a transient increase in turning and a more sustained increase in forward velocity and the fraction of flies moving when all bitter neurons were activated.
source: Activating the entire population of bitter neurons strongly stimulated locomotion at all light intensities. Light onset elicited a transient increase in turning and a more sustained increase in forward velocity and the fraction of flies moving (Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When light stimulation was turned off, flies immediately stopped moving, and this locomotor suppression persisted for nearly a minute.
source: When light stimulation was turned off, flies immediately stopped moving, and this locomotor suppression persisted for nearly a minute (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The same behavioral effects were observed with continuous light stimulation and 50 Hz pulsed light.
source: We observed the same behavioral effects with continuous light stimulation (Figure 3C–D) and 50 Hz pulsed light (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: When a fly senses a bitter stimulus, it displays a sequence of stereotyped behaviors mediating aversion: it first turns in an attempt to orient away from the stimulus, it increases forward velocity in an attempt to run away from the stimulus, and when the stimulus disappears, it freezes because it may perceive its current position to be a safe (bitter-free) location.
source: Together, these results suggest that when a fly senses a bitter stimulus, it displays a sequence of stereotyped behaviors mediating aversion: (1) it first turns in an attempt to orient away from the stimulus, (2) it increases forward velocity in an attempt to run away from the stimulus, and (3) when the stimulus disappears, it freezes because it may perceive its current position to be a safe (bitter-free) location.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the locomotor results.

claim: Activating any of the four bitter neuron subsets enhanced locomotion for at least one of the three light intensities.
source: Instead, activating any of the four bitter neuron subsets enhanced locomotion for at least one of the three light intensities (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Three of the four subsets (all except labellar S-b neurons) elicited an increase in turning at light onset as well as locomotor suppression after light was turned off, although the latter effect was only significant for two lines.
source: Three of the four subsets (all except labellar S-b neurons) also elicited an increase in turning at light onset as well as locomotor suppression after light was turned off, although the latter effect was only significant for two lines (Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bitter neurons in three different organs can drive locomotor changes typical of aversion.
source: These results show that bitter neurons in three different organs can drive locomotor changes typical of aversion, again suggesting that different bitter inputs converge onto common behavioral circuits.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the locomotor results.

claim: Flies avoid residing in areas containing bitter compounds.
source: Flies avoid residing in areas containing bitter compounds (Marella et al., 2006; Joseph and Heberlein, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marella et al., 2006 and Joseph and Heberlein, 2012.

claim: Expressing Chrimson in all bitter neurons elicited strong positional aversion at all light intensities.
source: Expressing Chrimson in all bitter neurons elicited strong positional aversion at all light intensities (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The effect of activating all bitter neurons on positional aversion was similar for continuous or 50 Hz pulsed light stimulation.
source: The effect was similar for continuous or 50 Hz pulsed light stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activating three of the four bitter neuron subsets elicited innate aversion.
source: We then tested the effect of each bitter neuron subset. Activating three of the four bitter neuron subsets elicited innate aversion (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activating three of the four bitter neuron subsets elicited innate aversion, including neuronal subsets in the leg, labellum, and pharynx, with only labellar S-b neurons failing to elicit an effect.
source: This included neuronal subsets in the leg, labellum, and pharynx, with only labellar S-b neurons failing to elicit an effect.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the innate aversion results.

claim: Bitter taste can serve as a negative reinforcement signal to elicit learned aversion to odors.
source: In addition to driving innate aversion, bitter taste can serve as a negative reinforcement signal to elicit learned aversion to odors (Das et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Das et al., 2014.

claim: Pairing odor with the activation of all bitter neurons elicited aversion to the CS+.
source: As expected, pairing odor with the activation of all bitter neurons elicited aversion to the CS+ (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Activating two of the four bitter neuron subsets elicited learned aversion, including neurons in the leg and labellum.
source: Activating two of the four bitter neuron subsets also elicited learned aversion (Figure 4F), including neurons in the leg and labellum.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Labellar S-b neurons failed to elicit a significant effect on learned aversion, similar to their lack of an effect on innate aversion.
source: Labellar S-b neurons failed to elicit a significant effect, similar to their lack of an effect on innate aversion.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the learned aversion results for labellar S-b neurons.

claim: Pharyngeal neurons did not elicit a learned response despite driving strong innate aversion.
source: Interestingly, pharyngeal neurons did not elicit a learned response despite driving strong innate aversion.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the learned aversion results for pharyngeal neurons.

claim: Different subsets of bitter neurons drive broad and largely overlapping behavioral responses.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that different subsets of bitter neurons drive broad and largely overlapping behavioral responses (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the behavioral results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The fact that all neuronal subsets strongly evoked at least one aversive behavior suggests that each set of neurons was effectively activated by Chrimson.
source: The fact that all neuronal subsets strongly evoked at least one aversive behavior suggests that each set of neurons was effectively activated by Chrimson.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the behavioral results.

claim: Labellar S-b neurons had the sparsest effect and only affected three of the seven behavioral measures analyzed.
source: Labellar S-b neurons had the sparsest effect and only affected three of the seven behavioral measures analyzed (Figure 5A), but we noted that the corresponding Gal4 line may have weaker expression than the other lines (based on weaker labeling of axonal projections in the brain and the inability to drive consistent trans-Tango labeling in the experiments below; data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and observations about Gal4 expression.

claim: The other three subsets, residing in three different organs, all affected at least six of the seven behaviors tested, including proboscis extension, feeding, locomotion, and innate aversion.
source: The other three subsets, residing in three different organs, all affected at least six of the seven behaviors tested, including proboscis extension, feeding, locomotion, and innate aversion (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Two of those three subsets (leg and labellar S-a + I-a neurons) also caused aversive learning.
source: Two of those three subsets (leg and labellar S-a + I-a neurons) also caused aversive learning.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the learning results.

claim: The results generally support an integrative model of taste processing in which bitter inputs from different organs converge onto common downstream pathways to drive a diverse set of aversive behaviors.
source: These results generally support an integrative model of taste processing (Figure 1B, left) in which bitter inputs from different organs converge onto common downstream pathways to drive a diverse set of aversive behaviors.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: The fact that not all neuronal subsets elicited all behaviors, or preferentially elicited some behaviors over others, suggests that some downstream pathways may receive selective or preferential input from specific bitter-sensing cells.
source: However, the fact that not all neuronal subsets elicited all behaviors, or preferentially elicited some behaviors over others, suggests that some downstream pathways may receive selective or preferential input from specific bitter-sensing cells.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: The model of selective integration lies in between the integrative and segregated processing models.
source: We refer to this model as 'selective integration' (Figure 5B), and it lies in between the two models shown in Figure 1B.
evidence: The claim is a description of the selective integration model.

claim: The entire population of second-order bitter neurons includes many local neurons projecting within the SEZ as well as three major projections to the superior protocerebrum: a lateral, medial, and mediolateral tract.
source: We first labeled the entire population of second-order bitter neurons by tracing neurons that are postsynaptic to Gr33a-Gal4-expressing cells. We observed many local neurons projecting within the SEZ as well as three major projections to the superior protocerebrum: a lateral, medial, and mediolateral tract (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango tracing data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: This pattern is consistent with second-order bitter neurons labeled in other recent studies.
source: This pattern is consistent with second-order bitter neurons labeled in other recent studies (Chen et al., 2019; Snell et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2019 and Snell et al., 2022.

claim: At the first synapse, the bitter taste circuit diverges into at least three downstream pathways projecting out of the SEZ.
source: Thus, at the first synapse, the bitter taste circuit diverges into at least three downstream pathways projecting out of the SEZ.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the trans-Tango tracing results.

claim: Tracing neurons postsynaptic to bitter cells in the leg labeled all three projection tracts, although the medial tract was labeled relatively weakly.
source: Tracing neurons postsynaptic to bitter cells in the leg labeled all three projection tracts, although the medial tract was labeled relatively weakly.
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango tracing data.

claim: Tracing from S-a + I-a neurons in the labellum also labeled all three tracts; the medial tract was labeled more strongly than when tracing from the leg, whereas the lateral tract was labeled more weakly.
source: Tracing from S-a + I-a neurons in the labellum also labeled all three tracts; the medial tract was labeled more strongly than when tracing from the leg, whereas the lateral tract was labeled more weakly.
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango tracing data.

claim: Tracing neurons postsynaptic to pharyngeal bitter neurons labeled the medial tract almost exclusively, although the mediolateral tract occasionally showed weak labeling.
source: Finally, tracing neurons postsynaptic to pharyngeal bitter neurons labeled the medial tract almost exclusively, although the mediolateral tract occasionally showed weak labeling.
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango tracing data.

claim: A previous study tracing postsynaptic partners of pharyngeal taste neurons reported similar results, although the mediolateral tract was more clearly labeled in that study.
source: A previous study tracing postsynaptic partners of pharyngeal taste neurons reported similar results, although the mediolateral tract was more clearly labeled in that study (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Bitter neurons in each organ synapse onto multiple second-order pathways.
source: Together, these results show that: (1) bitter neurons in each organ synapse onto multiple second-order pathways, and (2) each projection tract receives input from multiple organs, although it is not clear whether these inputs converge onto the same individual neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the trans-Tango tracing results.

claim: Each projection tract receives input from multiple organs, although it is not clear whether these inputs converge onto the same individual neurons.
source: Together, these results show that: (1) bitter neurons in each organ synapse onto multiple second-order pathways, and (2) each projection tract receives input from multiple organs, although it is not clear whether these inputs converge onto the same individual neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the trans-Tango tracing results.

claim: Bitter inputs show biased connectivity to second-order taste regions, with neurons in different organs preferentially connecting to different projection tracts.
source: Interestingly, bitter inputs show biased connectivity to second-order taste regions, with neurons in different organs preferentially connecting to different projection tracts (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the trans-Tango tracing results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: This biased connectivity could allow downstream taste pathways to be selectively or preferentially activated by certain organs, as suggested by the behavioral results.
source: This biased connectivity could allow downstream taste pathways to be selectively or preferentially activated by certain organs, as suggested by our behavioral results (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the trans-Tango tracing results and behavioral results.

claim: mlSEZt neurons have cell bodies just dorsal to the antennal lobes, a V-shaped projection in the SEZ, and a circular projection in the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP).
source: As visible in the first line we identified, R29F12-Gal4, mlSEZt neurons have cell bodies just dorsal to the antennal lobes, a V-shaped projection in the SEZ, and a circular projection in the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP) (Figure 7A, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by the expression pattern shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The axons of bitter-sensing neurons overlap with the medial branch of the mlSEZt projection in the SEZ.
source: Colabeling revealed that the axons of bitter-sensing neurons overlap with the medial branch of the mlSEZt projection in the SEZ (Figure 7A, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by colabeling data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: mlSEZt projections in both the SEZ and SLP responded to bitter stimulation of either the labellum or leg.
source: mlSEZt projections in both the SEZ and SLP responded to bitter stimulation of either the labellum or leg (Figure 7B–D), demonstrating that these neurons receive bitter input from multiple organs.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B–D.

claim: mlSEZt neurons receive bitter input from multiple organs.
source: mlSEZt projections in both the SEZ and SLP responded to bitter stimulation of either the labellum or leg (Figure 7B–D), demonstrating that these neurons receive bitter input from multiple organs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the calcium imaging data.

claim: Water or sugar applied to the labellum elicited a much weaker response than bitter in the SEZ (~50% of the bitter response) and no response in the SLP.
source: Water or sugar applied to the labellum elicited a much weaker response than bitter in the SEZ (~50% of the bitter response; Figure 7B) and no response in the SLP (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Water or sugar responses were not observed in either the SEZ or SLP with tarsal stimulation.
source: Water or sugar responses were not observed in either the SEZ or SLP with tarsal stimulation (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B–C.

claim: The addition of sugar did not modulate the response to labellar bitter stimulation.
source: The addition of sugar did not modulate the response to labellar bitter stimulation (Figure 7E), suggesting that mlSEZt neurons do not receive inhibition from the sugar pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: mlSEZt neurons do not receive inhibition from the sugar pathway.
source: The addition of sugar did not modulate the response to labellar bitter stimulation (Figure 7E), suggesting that mlSEZt neurons do not receive inhibition from the sugar pathway.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the calcium imaging data.

claim: mlSEZt neurons showed different response dynamics when bitter was applied to the labellum versus the leg, as previously reported for bitter sensory neurons in these organs.
source: mlSEZt neurons showed different response dynamics when bitter was applied to the labellum versus the leg, as previously reported for bitter sensory neurons in these organs (Devineni et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data and a citation to Devineni et al., 2021.

claim: Bitter stimulation of the labellum elicited transient responses at bitter onset (ON response) and offset (OFF response), whereas stimulation of the leg elicited a more sustained ON response with no OFF response.
source: Bitter stimulation of the labellum elicited transient responses at bitter onset (ON response) and offset (OFF response), whereas stimulation of the leg elicited a more sustained ON response with no OFF response (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B–D.

claim: Labellar stimulation elicited stronger ON responses than tarsal stimulation (~70% versus ~30% ∆F/F).
source: When comparing responses in the same flies (Figure 7D), labellar stimulation elicited stronger ON responses than tarsal stimulation (~70% versus ~30% ∆F/F).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Tarsal and labellar bitter stimulation produced different spatial patterns of activation in the SEZ.
source: Tarsal and labellar bitter stimulation also produced different spatial patterns of activation in the SEZ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Responses to tarsal stimulation were localized to a small region located at the dorsolateral edge of the larger region activated by labellar stimulation.
source: Responses to tarsal stimulation were localized to a small region located at the dorsolateral edge of the larger region activated by labellar stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: This is consistent with the colabeling experiment and the known projection patterns of tarsal and labellar bitter-sensing neurons.
source: This is consistent with our colabeling experiment (Figure 7A, bottom) and the known projection patterns of tarsal and labellar bitter-sensing neurons (Wang et al., 2004; Kwon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by the colabeling experiment and citations to Wang et al., 2004 and Kwon et al., 2014.

claim: Bitter inputs from different organs likely activate different dendrites on mlSEZt neurons.
source: Thus, bitter inputs from different organs likely activate different dendrites on mlSEZt neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the spatial patterns of activation in the SEZ.

claim: In the SLP, the spatial pattern of mlSEZt activation was similar when bitter was applied to either the leg or labellum.
source: In the SLP, the spatial pattern of mlSEZt activation was similar when bitter was applied to either the leg or labellum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Individual puncta, likely representing axon terminals of single mlSEZt cells, were activated by bitter stimulation of either organ.
source: We observed individual puncta, likely representing axon terminals of single mlSEZt cells, that were activated by bitter stimulation of either organ.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: These results suggest that individual mlSEZt cells receive convergent input from the labellum and leg.
source: These results suggest that individual mlSEZt cells receive convergent input from the labellum and leg.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the calcium imaging data.

claim: mlSEZt neurons showed compound-dependent dynamics that resembled those of sensory neurons.
source: Indeed, mlSEZt neurons showed compound-dependent dynamics that resembled those of sensory neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Relative to the strength of the ON response, denatonium and quinine elicited strong OFF responses, caffeine elicited a slightly weaker OFF response, and L-canavanine elicited no OFF response at all.
source: Relative to the strength of the ON response, denatonium and quinine elicited strong OFF responses, caffeine elicited a slightly weaker OFF response, and L-canavanine elicited no OFF response at all (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: mlSEZt responses showed an experience-dependent effect resembling that of bitter-sensing neurons: with repeated bitter stimulation, the bitter ON response habituated much more strongly than the OFF response.
source: mlSEZt responses also showed an experience-dependent effect resembling that of bitter-sensing neurons: with repeated bitter stimulation, the bitter ON response habituated much more strongly than the OFF response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The mlSEZt neurons labeled by R29F12-Gal4 are second-order bitter neurons.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that the mlSEZt neurons labeled by R29F12-Gal4 are second-order bitter neurons: they have an identical morphology to second-order bitter neurons labeled by trans-Tango, their projections overlap with the axon terminals of bitter-sensing neurons, and they show clear bitter responses.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on morphology, overlap with bitter-sensing neurons, and calcium imaging data.

claim: It is formally possible that mlSEZt neurons are downstream bitter neurons that are not directly connected to bitter-sensing cells.
source: We will therefore refer to mlSEZt neurons as second-order bitter neurons, although it is formally possible that they are downstream bitter neurons that are not directly connected to bitter-sensing cells.
evidence: The claim acknowledges an alternative interpretation.

claim: The taste selectivity and response dynamics of mlSEZt neurons closely resemble those of bitter sensory neurons.
source: The taste selectivity and response dynamics of mlSEZt neurons closely resemble those of bitter sensory neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the calcium imaging results.

claim: The major transformation observed in mlSEZt neurons is that they receive convergent bitter input from at least two different organs, the leg and labellum.
source: The major transformation we observe is that mlSEZt neurons receive convergent bitter input from at least two different organs, the leg and labellum.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the calcium imaging results.

claim: This convergence may represent a substrate by which bitter neurons in different organs elicit common behavioral effects.
source: This convergence may represent a substrate by which bitter neurons in different organs elicit common behavioral effects (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the calcium imaging results and behavioral results.

claim: Activating mlSEZt neurons suppressed PER to sugar.
source: Activating mlSEZt neurons using Chrimson suppressed PER to sugar (Figure 8B), similar to the effect of activating bitter-sensing neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Silencing mlSEZt neurons reduced the PER suppression elicited by quinine.
source: Silencing mlSEZt neurons using GTACR reduced the PER suppression elicited by quinine (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: mlSEZt neurons partially mediate the aversive effect of bitter taste on proboscis extension.
source: Thus, mlSEZt neurons partially mediate the aversive effect of bitter taste on proboscis extension.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the PER results.

claim: mlSEZt activation suppressed feeding on sugar.
source: mlSEZt activation suppressed feeding on sugar (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B), consistent with its effect on PER.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Certain feeding parameters were suppressed by mlSEZt activation (e.g., total feeding duration, sip duration, number of feeding bouts) while others were not (e.g., number of sips).
source: Certain feeding parameters were suppressed (e.g., total feeding duration, sip duration, number of feeding bouts) while others were not (e.g., number of sips).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the feeding results.

claim: mlSEZt silencing did not significantly affect feeding on a sugar/bitter mixture.
source: In contrast to the effect of activation, mlSEZt silencing did not significantly affect feeding on a sugar/bitter mixture (Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: mlSEZt neurons suppress specific aspects of feeding behavior but act in parallel with other second-order bitter pathways, creating redundancy in the circuit.
source: These results suggest that mlSEZt neurons suppress specific aspects of feeding behavior but act in parallel with other second-order bitter pathways, creating redundancy in the circuit.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the feeding results.

claim: Activating mlSEZt neurons generally did not elicit locomotor changes, innate positional aversion, or learned aversion.
source: In contrast to the effect on proboscis extension and feeding, activating mlSEZt neurons generally did not elicit locomotor changes, innate positional aversion, or learned aversion (Figure 8F–H and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8F–H and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The only statistically significant effect in any of these behavioral assays, at any light intensity, was an increase in turning at the onset of high intensity light.
source: The only statistically significant effect in any of these behavioral assays, at any light intensity, was an increase in turning at the onset of high intensity light (Figure 8F); medium intensity light also elicited a similar but non-significant effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Changes in forward velocity at light onset or offset did not differ from controls.
source: Changes in forward velocity at light onset or offset did not differ from controls (Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: None of the locomotor or preference behaviors elicited by bitter sensory activation were affected by mlSEZt silencing.
source: None of the locomotor or preference behaviors elicited by bitter sensory activation were affected by mlSEZt silencing (Figure 8—figure supplement 3), indicating that mlSEZt neurons are not required for these behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: mlSEZt neurons are not required for locomotor or preference behaviors elicited by bitter sensory activation.
source: None of the locomotor or preference behaviors elicited by bitter sensory activation were affected by mlSEZt silencing (Figure 8—figure supplement 3), indicating that mlSEZt neurons are not required for these behaviors.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the silencing results.

claim: Second-order mlSEZt neurons regulate a subset of the aversive behaviors elicited by bitter taste.
source: Together, these data show that second-order mlSEZt neurons regulate a subset of the aversive behaviors elicited by bitter taste.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the behavioral results for mlSEZt neurons.

claim: Behaviors that were not affected by mlSEZt activation may be mediated by other second-order bitter pathways, or they may require the co-activation of multiple second-order pathways.
source: Behaviors that were not affected by mlSEZt activation may be mediated by other second-order bitter pathways, or they may require the co-activation of multiple second-order pathways.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the role of other second-order pathways.

claim: The morphology of mlSEZt neurons indicates that they belong to the CREa1 lineage.
source: The morphology of mlSEZt neurons indicates that they belong to the CREa1 lineage (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Neurons within the CREa1 lineage have sexually dimorphic projections.
source: Neurons within this lineage have sexually dimorphic projections (Yu et al., 2013), and mlSEZt neurons share some resemblance with sexually dimorphic fruitless (fru)-expressing mAL (aDT2) neurons (Kimura et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2010; Cachero et al., 2010), which function in the male courtship circuit (Clowney et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2013.

claim: mlSEZt neurons share some resemblance with sexually dimorphic fruitless (fru)-expressing mAL (aDT2) neurons, which function in the male courtship circuit.
source: Neurons within this lineage have sexually dimorphic projections (Yu et al., 2013), and mlSEZt neurons share some resemblance with sexually dimorphic fruitless (fru)-expressing mAL (aDT2) neurons (Kimura et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2010; Cachero et al., 2010), which function in the male courtship circuit (Clowney et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kimura et al., 2005, Yu et al., 2010, Cachero et al., 2010, and Clowney et al., 2015.

claim: mAL neurons in males do not have a circular projection in the SLP, as mlSEZt cells do.
source: However, mAL neurons in males do not have a circular projection in the SLP, as mlSEZt cells do.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of mAL neuron morphology.

claim: mlSEZt neurons in males also show a circular SLP projection, indicating that they are distinct from fru+mAL neurons and do not appear to be sexually dimorphic.
source: Although our initial characterization of mlSEZt neurons was performed in females (Figures 7–8), mlSEZt neurons in males also show a circular SLP projection (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that they are distinct from fru+mAL neurons and do not appear to be sexually dimorphic.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CREa1 lineage contains GABAergic neurons.
source: The CREa1 lineage contains GABAergic neurons (Ito et al., 2013), and some neurons resembling mlSEZt in the FlyCircuit database express Gad1-Gal4, a GABAergic marker (e.g., Gad1-F-600213 and Gad1-F-400450) (Chiang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ito et al., 2013.

claim: Some neurons resembling mlSEZt in the FlyCircuit database express Gad1-Gal4, a GABAergic marker.
source: The CREa1 lineage contains GABAergic neurons (Ito et al., 2013), and some neurons resembling mlSEZt in the FlyCircuit database express Gad1-Gal4, a GABAergic marker (e.g., Gad1-F-600213 and Gad1-F-400450) (Chiang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chiang et al., 2011.

claim: Most mlSEZt cells co-express VGAT-lexA, a GABAergic marker.
source: To confirm that mlSEZt cells are GABAergic, we colabeled them with the GABAergic marker VGAT-lexA and observed co-expression in most mlSEZt cells (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by colabeling data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No mlSEZt neurons expressed ChAT-lexA, a cholinergic marker.
source: We did not observe any mlSEZt neurons that expressed ChAT-lexA (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colabeling data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 2B.

claim: mlSEZt bitter neurons are GABAergic cells that convey feedforward inhibition to the SLP.
source: Thus, mlSEZt bitter neurons are GABAergic cells that convey feedforward inhibition to the SLP.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the colabeling data.

claim: mlSEZt neurons themselves were prominently labeled in trans-Tango experiments, suggesting that they form connections with each other.
source: Interestingly, mlSEZt neurons themselves were prominently labeled (Figure 9B), suggesting that they form connections with each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Dense staining was observed in the SLP and the neighboring superior intermediate protocerebrum (SIP), with many cell bodies located laterally.
source: We also observed dense staining in the SLP and the neighboring superior intermediate protocerebrum (SIP), with many cell bodies located laterally (Figure 9B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango data shown in Figure 9B–C.

claim: There were very few projections out of the SLP/SIP, suggesting that 3Ns primarily comprise local neurons.
source: There were very few projections out of the SLP/SIP, suggesting that 3Ns primarily comprise local neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the trans-Tango data.

claim: The few projections out of the SLP/SIP mainly arborize in the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP), the region innervated by second-order bitter neurons comprising the medial tract, which suggests potential cross-talk between different second-order pathways.
source: The few projections out of the SLP/SIP mainly arborize in the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP) (Figure 9C), the region innervated by second-order bitter neurons comprising the medial tract (Figure 6), which suggests potential cross-talk between different second-order pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango data shown in Figure 9C and an inference about cross-talk.

claim: A medial projection crossed the midline and innervated the contralateral SLP/SIP.
source: We also observed a medial projection that crossed the midline and innervated the contralateral SLP/SIP (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: A single projection descended vertically from the SMP along the midline, potentially innervating the SEZ, and another projection descended directly from the SLP to the ventral brain.
source: Finally, we observed a single projection that descended vertically from the SMP along the midline, potentially innervating the SEZ, and another projection descending directly from the SLP to the ventral brain (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-Tango data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: 21 neurons in the connectome whose morphology strongly resembled that of mlSEZt cells were identified.
source: We identified 21 neurons whose morphology strongly resembled that of mlSEZt cells (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectome analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: These neurons were classified in the connectome as three different cell types: mAL3A (6 cells), mAL3B (5 cells), and mAL4 (10 cells).
source: These neurons were classified in the connectome as three different cell types: mAL3A (6 cells), mAL3B (5 cells), and mAL4 (10 cells).
evidence: The claim is based on connectome classification.

claim: All three cell types show a ring-shaped projection in the SLP, with subtle differences in their arborizations.
source: All three cell types show a ring-shaped projection in the SLP, with subtle differences in their arborizations (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectome data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Four of the ten 3Ns receiving the strongest mlSEZt input are in fact mlSEZt cells, revealing strong interconnectivity.
source: Interestingly, four of the ten 3Ns receiving the strongest mlSEZt input are in fact mlSEZt cells, revealing strong interconnectivity that is consistent with trans-Tango labeling (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectome analysis and trans-Tango data.

claim: There are many strong connections from mAL3A to mAL3B, a few connections in the opposite direction (mAL3B to mAL3A), a few connections from mAL3A or mAL3B to mAL4, and almost no connections from mAL4 to the other types.
source: There are many strong connections from mAL3A to mAL3B, a few connections in the opposite direction (mAL3B to mAL3A), a few connections from mAL3A or mAL3B to mAL4, and almost no connections from mAL4 to the other types (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectome analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: These results suggest a hierarchy where mAL3A strongly influences mAL3B, mAL3A and mAL3B weakly influence mAL4, and mAL4 does not influence the other types.
source: These results suggest a hierarchy where mAL3A strongly influences mAL3B, mAL3A and mAL3B weakly influence mAL4, and mAL4 does not influence the other types.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the connectome analysis.

claim: Because these cells are GABAergic, these interactions may mediate inhibitory cross-talk that dampens or gates the responses of other mlSEZt cells.
source: Because these cells are GABAergic, these interactions may mediate inhibitory cross-talk that dampens or gates the responses of other mlSEZt cells.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the GABAergic nature of mlSEZt cells.

claim: Most of the 3Ns receiving the strongest mlSEZt input are neurons projecting locally within the SLP and SIP, consistent with trans-Tango staining.
source: After excluding interconnections between mlSEZt cells, most of the 3Ns receiving the strongest mlSEZt input are neurons projecting locally within the SLP and SIP (Figure 9F–H and Table 1), consistent with trans-Tango staining (Figure 9B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectome analysis and trans-Tango data.

claim: Other areas targeted by top 3Ns include nearby regions such as the SMP, lateral horn, superior clamp, and anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum.
source: Other areas targeted by top 3Ns include nearby regions such as the SMP, lateral horn, superior clamp, and anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum.
evidence: The claim is based on connectome analysis.

claim: Very few 3Ns have long-range projections.
source: Very few 3Ns have long-range projections.
evidence: The claim is based on connectome analysis.

claim: Different mlSEZt cell types show different connectivity patterns to the top 3Ns.
source: Different mlSEZt cell types show different connectivity patterns to the top 3Ns (Figure 9G).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectome analysis shown in Figure 9G.

claim: mAL3A cells provide the weakest input to the top 3Ns despite providing the strongest input to other mlSEZt cells, suggesting a distinction between lateral and feedforward mlSEZt circuitry.
source: Interestingly, mAL3A cells provide the weakest input to the top 3Ns (Figure 9G) despite providing the strongest input to other mlSEZt cells (Figure 9E), suggesting a distinction between lateral and feedforward mlSEZt circuitry.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on connectome analysis shown in Figure 9G and 9E.

claim: Most of the top 3Ns have not been previously studied, but some have been identified in other connectomic studies.
source: Most of the top 3Ns (Table 1) have not been previously studied, but some have been identified in other connectomic studies.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of previous studies.

claim: Two top 3N types (SLP259 and SLP018) are third-order olfactory neurons in a pheromone-sensing circuit.
source: Two top 3N types (SLP259 and SLP018) are third-order olfactory neurons in a pheromone-sensing circuit (Taisz et al., 2022) and one top 3N, LHCENT1, connects the mushroom body to olfactory circuits in the lateral horn (Bates et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taisz et al., 2022 and Bates et al., 2020.

claim: One top 3N, LHCENT1, connects the mushroom body to olfactory circuits in the lateral horn.
source: Two top 3N types (SLP259 and SLP018) are third-order olfactory neurons in a pheromone-sensing circuit (Taisz et al., 2022) and one top 3N, LHCENT1, connects the mushroom body to olfactory circuits in the lateral horn (Bates et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bates et al., 2020.

claim: Several other 3Ns are lateral horn neurons that may participate in olfactory processing.
source: Several other 3Ns are lateral horn neurons that may participate in olfactory processing (Schlegel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schlegel et al., 2021.

claim: mlSEZt cells likely provide input to neurons integrating olfactory and gustatory information.
source: Thus, mlSEZt neurons likely provide input to neurons integrating olfactory and gustatory information.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the identity of 3Ns.

claim: mlSEZt cells (mAL3) as well as several other second-order taste neurons were identified as inputs to aSP-g3, suggesting that some 3Ns integrate input from multiple types of second-order neurons.
source: The inputs to another top 3N type, aSP-g3, were recently reconstructed using a whole-brain connectome dataset (Taisz et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2018). mlSEZt cells (mAL3) as well as several other second-order taste neurons were identified as inputs to aSP-g3, suggesting that some 3Ns integrate input from multiple types of second-order neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taisz et al., 2022 and Zheng et al., 2018.

claim: The 4Ns include several mlSEZt cells, revealing feedback connections that likely modulate mlSEZt output.
source: The 4Ns include several mlSEZt cells, revealing feedback connections that likely modulate mlSEZt output.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on connectome analysis.

claim: Most of the top 4Ns send axonal projections to the SLP, SIP, or nearby areas, but collectively they target more diverse brain regions than the 3Ns.
source: Most of these top 4Ns send axonal projections to the SLP, SIP, or nearby areas, but collectively they target more diverse brain regions than the 3Ns (Figure 9I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectome analysis shown in Figure 9I–J.

claim: 4N projections to the SMP are especially prominent, with 90% of top 4Ns sending output to this region.
source: 4N projections to the SMP are especially prominent, with 90% of top 4Ns sending output to this region.
evidence: The claim is based on connectome analysis.

claim: 60% of the top 4Ns project to the lateral horn and 43% project to the mushroom body, regions that mediate innate and learned olfactory processing, respectively.
source: 60% of the top 4Ns project to the lateral horn and 43% project to the mushroom body, regions that mediate innate and learned olfactory processing, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on connectome analysis and knowledge of brain region functions.

claim: The top 4Ns include neurons that regulate egg-laying (oviIN and oviDNa; two oviDNb cells are also 4Ns but not in the top 30).
source: The top 4Ns include neurons that regulate egg-laying (oviIN and oviDNa; two oviDNb cells are also 4Ns but not in the top 30; Wang et al., 2020), mushroom body output neurons (Aso et al., 2014a), and the PPL201 (PPL2a) dopaminergic neuron (Li et al., 2020; Boto et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020, Aso et al., 2014a, Li et al., 2020, and Boto et al., 2019.

claim: The 322 4Ns receiving strong 3N input do not include PPL1 dopaminergic neurons, which convey bitter information to the mushroom body for aversive learning, and this may correlate with the inability of mlSEZt cells to elicit learned aversion.
source: The 322 4Ns receiving strong 3N input do not include PPL1 dopaminergic neurons, which convey bitter information to the mushroom body for aversive learning (Kirkhart and Scott, 2015), and this may correlate with the inability of mlSEZt cells to elicit learned aversion (Figure 8H).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on connectome analysis and behavioral results, supported by a citation to Kirkhart and Scott, 2015.

claim: Bitter inputs from different organs are integrated early in the circuit and drive largely overlapping behaviors, contrasting with the prevailing view that different taste organs have different functions.
source: Together, these results suggest that bitter inputs from different organs are selectively integrated at the first synapse and drive largely overlapping behaviors, contrasting with the prevailing view that different taste organs have different functions.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The studies provide insight into the functional role of downstream bitter neurons and the organization of taste pathways in the higher brain.
source: Our studies also provide insight into the functional role of downstream bitter neurons and the organization of taste pathways in the higher brain.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the contributions of the study.
